name: Reinspection
summary: Step-by-step process from identifying the issue through follow-up.
whenToUse: Use this when you believe the carrier's inspection missed damage, was incomplete, or new documentation has come to light since it happened.
whatToCheck: Do you have clear photo or measurement evidence of what was missed?
Is the original estimate/report available to reference?
Has reinspection already been requested and denied? (If so, see the Reinspection Denied scenario instead.)

steps.title: Identify exactly what was missed
steps.detail: Pin down the specific area(s) or item(s) you believe weren't captured — vague requests get vague responses.

steps.title: Gather supporting documentation
steps.detail: Photos, measurements, or reports that clearly show the disputed damage.

steps.title: Send the reinspection request
steps.detail: Use the Reinspection Request template. Name the specific items in dispute and attach documentation.

steps.title: Log the request
steps.detail: Record the request, date, and what was disputed in Contractors Cloud.

steps.title: Follow up if needed
steps.detail: If you haven't heard back within a reasonable window, send a follow-up using the Reinspection Follow-Up template.

steps.title: Review the outcome
steps.detail: If granted and completed, confirm the updated scope reflects what was found. If denied, move to the Reinspection Denied scenario.

followUp: 1-2 weeks after the request if no response; check in with the client if the reinspection date affects their timeline.
escalation: Escalate if reinspection is flatly denied without explanation, or delayed repeatedly with no firm date.

name: Appraisal
summary: Step-by-step process from identifying appraisal as an option through demand, appraiser coordination, award, carrier follow-up, and closeout.
whenToUse: Use this when standard negotiation on the amount of loss has stalled — the carrier isn't disputing coverage, but you and the carrier can't close the gap on scope or price.
whatToCheck: Is this genuinely a dispute over amount, not coverage?
Have reasonable attempts already been made to resolve it directly (documentation, reinspection, pushing the estimate)?
Has the client been informed and does the policy support appraisal?

steps.title: Confirm appraisal is the right path
steps.detail: Make sure this is an amount dispute, not a coverage dispute — appraisal doesn't resolve coverage questions.

steps.title: Notify the client
steps.detail: Explain what appraisal means in plain terms. Use the Client Explanation of Appraisal template.

steps.title: Prepare the demand package
steps.detail: Compile the estimate comparison and documentation, and select an appraiser from your roster.

steps.title: Send the demand letter
steps.detail: Formally invoke the appraisal clause, naming your selected appraiser.

steps.title: Track the carrier's response
steps.detail: Confirm they've named their own appraiser.

steps.title: Follow up during appraisal
steps.detail: Check in with your appraiser roughly every 2-3 weeks if you haven't heard updates.

steps.title: Handle any pushback
steps.detail: If the client has doubts or objections during the process, work through them directly rather than letting it stall.

steps.title: Receive the award
steps.detail: Once an award is issued, follow up with the carrier on settlement and payment the same day.

steps.title: Close out
steps.detail: Complete revised-estimate, payment-tracking, and next-step handoffs; record the outcome; confirm the client is updated.

followUp: 2-3 weeks with your appraiser during active appraisal; same-day carrier follow-up once an award is received.
escalation: Escalate high-value or complex claims to your lead before invoking appraisal, and any point where the process itself (not just the amount) is being disputed.

name: Denial
summary: How to analyze a denial and determine the appropriate next move.
whenToUse: Use this any time a claim comes back fully or partially denied, to work out whether it's a documentation problem or a coverage problem before doing anything else.
whatToCheck: What exact reason does the denial letter give?
Is this a dispute about whether there's covered damage, or whether it's covered at all?
What's already in the file, and what's missing?

steps.title: Read the denial closely
steps.detail: Identify the stated reason — wear and tear, prior damage, no storm damage, insufficient documentation, or a coverage question.

steps.title: Sort the dispute
steps.detail: Coverage disputes (is this covered at all) usually need escalation. Amount/damage disputes (is there covered damage here) are documentation, reinspection, or appraisal territory.

steps.title: Build the response
steps.detail: Gather the specific documentation that answers the carrier's stated reason — see the Documentation playbook.

steps.title: Submit and track
steps.detail: Send the response, log it, and set a follow-up.

steps.title: Reassess if it doesn't move
steps.detail: If a well-documented response doesn't change the outcome, escalate or consider appraisal depending on the type of dispute.

followUp: 3-5 business days to begin working a denial; 1-2 weeks after submitting a response.
escalation: Escalate immediately if the denial is a coverage dispute rather than a documentation/amount dispute.

name: Underpayment
summary: How to identify scope gaps and determine how to challenge them.
whenToUse: Use this when a claim was approved but the scope or dollar amount is lower than the actual repair requires.
whatToCheck: Where exactly does your estimate diverge from the carrier's — scope, quantity, or price?
Which differences are factual (a missed item, a wrong measurement) versus judgment calls (pricing, necessity)?
Is there a supplement process available for specific missing items?

steps.title: Build a side-by-side comparison
steps.detail: Line up your estimate against theirs, item by item.

steps.title: Separate factual gaps from judgment calls
steps.detail: Lead with the factual discrepancies — they're usually easier to resolve.

steps.title: Gather supporting documentation
steps.detail: Measurements, manufacturer info, or code documentation for disputed items.

steps.title: Submit the comparison
steps.detail: Send it as a clear, itemized request — either a supplement or a reconsideration.

steps.title: Follow up
steps.detail: 1-2 weeks if you haven't heard back.

steps.title: Escalate the path if it stalls
steps.detail: If the carrier won't move on a well-documented comparison, this is a strong appraisal candidate.

escalation: Escalate if the underpayment is large enough to affect whether the repair can be completed as scoped.

name: Documentation
summary: What documentation may be useful depending on the situation.
whenToUse: Use this as a reference any time you need to figure out what evidence would actually move a specific dispute forward.
whatToCheck: What is the carrier's exact stated objection or reason?
What documentation type would directly answer that specific objection — not just "more documentation" in general?
Does something like it already exist in the file?

steps.title: Photos
steps.detail: For damage, matching, and material disputes — clear, well-lit, and specific to the disputed item or area.

steps.title: Measurements
steps.detail: For scope and quantity disputes.

steps.title: Manufacturer information
steps.detail: For material, matching, and discontinuation disputes.

steps.title: ITEL / RLS / NTS
steps.detail: For material availability and matching disputes — see the ITEL Required scenario.

steps.title: Contractor estimate
steps.detail: To support scope and pricing positions.

steps.title: Code documentation
steps.detail: For code-upgrade related scope disputes — get the specific citation.

steps.title: Matching documentation
steps.detail: For disputes over whether materials need to match adjacent areas.

steps.title: Storm documentation
steps.detail: For wear-and-tear, prior-damage, and no-storm-damage arguments — ties damage to a specific dated event.

followUp: Varies by claim — see the specific scenario.
escalation: Escalate if you're unsure what documentation type actually applies to a given dispute.

name: Client Follow-Up
summary: How to handle stalled or unresponsive clients.
whenToUse: Use this when a claim needs client input or action and they've gone quiet, or seem hesitant about a next step.
whatToCheck: How long has it been, and through how many channels have you tried?
Is there an alternate contact on file?
Is this a time-sensitive step (like an appraisal deadline)?

steps.title: Send a clear, specific outreach
steps.detail: State exactly what's needed and by when — avoid vague "just checking in" messages.

steps.title: Try multiple channels
steps.detail: Call, text, and email if one channel alone hasn't worked.

steps.title: Try an alternate contact
steps.detail: If one exists and the primary contact is unreachable.

steps.title: Set a clear deadline in writing
steps.detail: Especially if a time-sensitive step is at risk.

steps.title: Escalate if needed
steps.detail: If a deadline is genuinely at risk, loop in your lead for guidance.

followUp: Every 3-5 business days while unresponsive; sooner if time-sensitive.
escalation: Escalate if client unresponsiveness threatens to cause a missed deadline.

name: Carrier Follow-Up
summary: How and when to follow up with the carrier.
whenToUse: Use this any time you're waiting on the carrier — a response, a reinspection date, a decision, or payment.
whatToCheck: What exactly are you waiting on, and how long has it been?
Have you already followed up once? What did they say, if anything?
Is there a deadline or urgency to factor in?

steps.title: Send a specific, dated follow-up
steps.detail: Reference the original request and restate exactly what you need.

steps.title: Use the right channel
steps.detail: If email hasn't worked, try phone, or vice versa.

steps.title: Log every attempt
steps.detail: Keep a clear record — this matters if you need to escalate later.

steps.title: Escalate after a reasonable pattern
steps.detail: Generally 2+ unanswered attempts over 1-2 weeks, sooner if urgent.

followUp: Every 3-5 business days while waiting on a response.
escalation: Escalate after 2+ unanswered follow-ups, or immediately if a deadline is at risk.
